claims.text: The investigated material is Q235 steel in an as-received, pre-exposure state with its native microstructure and surface finish.
Laser surface patterning will produce a higher density of surface micro-defects than mechanical polishing.
EBSD, stress analysis, and composition mapping can be used to verify whether defect density is changed without significant microstructural, stress, or chemical changes.
The controlled exposure will compare polished and laser-patterned samples in 3.5 wt% NaCl at approximately 25°C and 75°C for identical durations.
Surface micro-defects alter local electrochemical potentials.
High surface-defect densities provide preferential anodic sites.
Preferential sites associated with surface defects promote localized corrosion.
High surface-defect density causes early localized breakdown of the passive oxide film on Q235 steel.
Passive-film breakdown leads to active localized corrosion through enhanced charge-transfer processes.
Enhanced corrosion-related charge transfer is evidenced by decreased EIS polarization resistance.
A defect-minimized surface stabilizes the passive film and delays corrosion onset.
Laser-patterned Q235 samples will exhibit lower polarization resistance than polished samples.
Laser-patterned Q235 samples will exhibit a higher charge-transfer rate than polished samples.
Laser-patterned Q235 samples will develop localized corrosion features, including pits, earlier than polished samples.
The predicted defect-associated acceleration of corrosion will occur at both approximately 25°C and 75°C.
Surface roughness and inhomogeneity affect EIS spectra, while EIS time constants and semicircle evolution contain information about charge transfer and corrosion-product films.
Residual stress and subtle chemical changes introduced by laser treatment could confound the proposed defect-density effect.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to 3.5 wt% NaCl at approximately 25°C and 75°C and is not claimed for other electrolytes or temperatures.

A lack of statistically significant differences in polarization resistance, charge-transfer behavior, and corrosion morphology between patterned and polished samples at both temperatures would refute the proposed causal link.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as as-received with its native surface finish, but the baseline is called both untreated and polished. Mechanical polishing changes the as-received surface and therefore cannot simultaneously be an untreated native-finish reference.
